title: Public and Private Subnets

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn public and private subnets in the context of AWS Networking and Amazon VPC. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Public and Private Subnets matters because it is one part of amazon vpc and network reachability. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: VPC routing and network controls
content_blocks.alt_text: Reachability combines subnet routing, a route target, addressability, security groups, network ACLs and service-specific controls.
content_blocks.caption: A route alone does not prove reachability; all relevant network and identity controls matter.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Public and Private Subnets belongs to AWS Networking and Amazon VPC. VPC reachability is an end-to-end result of address ranges, subnet associations, routes, gateways, security groups, network ACLs and service endpoints—not just one firewall rule.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Public subnet routing requirements; Private application subnets; Isolated subnets; Separating public and private resources. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For public and private subnets, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Public subnet routing requirements
items.text: Trace the path from source to destination through address ranges, routing, gateways and filtering controls. Verify both forward and return paths; one successful configuration screen is not proof of reachability.

items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Public versus private subnet
content_blocks.code:
PUBLIC subnet: route to an Internet Gateway + appropriate addressing and security rules
PRIVATE subnet: no direct inbound internet route; outbound access may use NAT or service endpoints
ISOLATED subnet: no general internet route
content_blocks.expected_output: Subnet names alone do not create reachability; the associated route table and address/controls determine behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.
